abstract: Intersexual genetic correlation (IGC) is pervasive in sexually reproducing organisms and can constrain sex-specific adaptive evolution. Nevertheless, sexes frequently undergo adaptive divergence in response to novel ecological challenges. Here, we investigated whether adaptation to nutritional stress is sex-limited or constrained by shared genetic architecture. We utilized four laboratory-adapted populations of Drosophila melanogaster subjected to experimental evolution under adult-stage live-yeast deprivation for over 140 generations - a regime that previously drove adaptive female reproductive evolution, particularly enhancing early-life fecundity and ovarian function. Because female D. melanogaster rely heavily on dietary yeast for protein-dependent egg production, this evolutionary response may be female-limited. Alternatively, male fitness traits could respond either through direct selection or via correlated response driven by IGC. To distinguish between these hypotheses, we evaluated a comprehensive suite of pre- and post-copulatory male competitive fitness components. We found that all measured male fitness traits remained unchanged following experimental evolution, demonstrating that nutrient-dependent adaptation in these populations is strictly female-specific, with no evidence of correlated responses or sexually antagonistic trade-offs. Our results indicate that the genetic architecture underlying nutrient-dependent reproductive adaptation is largely decoupled between the sexes, allowing each sex to independently approach its sex-specific fitness optimum.
